letter.title: Understanding Evergreen Alternative Funds
paragraphs: Private markets have long been a part of building durable, diversified portfolios. In recent years, a newer structure has become more widely available: the evergreen alternative fund. This letter explains what these vehicles are, how they work, and how they differ from the closed-end private funds many of you already hold.

A traditional closed-end private fund raises capital once, invests it over a defined period, and returns capital to investors as holdings are sold, typically over the better part of a decade or more. Once committed, capital is generally locked up until the fund winds down.

An evergreen fund is structured differently. It does not have a fixed end date. Instead, it offers periodic windows, often monthly or quarterly, during which investors may subscribe additional capital or request redemptions. These are sometimes called continuous or perpetual-life funds.

It is important to understand what periodic liquidity means in practice. It is not the same as daily liquidity in a public mutual fund. Redemption requests are typically satisfied out of a limited pool set aside for that purpose, and the fund can apply caps, gates, or delays if requests in a given period exceed what it can accommodate. In periods of market stress, these limits are more likely to bind, and an investor wanting to exit may find that only a portion of their request is honored, with the remainder carried to a future period.

In exchange for this structure, evergreen funds can offer more flexibility than closed-end vehicles, allowing capital to be committed or withdrawn over time rather than locked to a single vintage. They also allow a manager to hold investments longer, without the pressure of a fixed liquidation date, which changes how and when assets are bought and sold.

The main risks to understand are liquidity risk, since redemptions are never guaranteed in full or on a fixed timeline, valuation risk, since these funds typically hold assets that are priced periodically rather than continuously, and structural risk, since the terms governing subscriptions, redemptions, and fees can vary meaningfully from one fund to another.

This letter is meant as background, not a recommendation. Whether an evergreen structure fits alongside your existing private equity and real estate holdings depends on your own liquidity needs and time horizon. We would welcome the chance to discuss this with you directly.

talking_points: Evergreen funds do not have a fixed end date, unlike traditional closed-end private funds.
They offer periodic windows, often monthly or quarterly, for subscriptions and redemptions.
Periodic liquidity is not the same as daily liquidity. The fund can limit, delay, or gate redemptions.
Client question: Can I always get my money out when I ask? Answer: No. Redemptions are typically capped and can be delayed if requests exceed what the fund sets aside for that purpose.

Client question: How is this different from the private equity I already own? Answer: Your existing funds are closed-end with a defined life; evergreen funds are open-ended with recurring, but limited, liquidity windows.
Client question: Does this mean it's safer or more conservative? Answer: No. It changes the liquidity structure, not the underlying risk of the assets held.
Valuations in these funds are typically set periodically, not continuously, which is a different pricing risk than public markets.
This is background information only. Any decision should be discussed one on one based on your own liquidity needs and time horizon.
Marchetti Ruiz Family Advisors.tailoring: Given that Marchetti Ruiz Family Advisors' clients already hold private equity and real estate, the letter frames evergreen funds specifically in contrast to the closed-end structures they already know, without recommending any allocation.

letter.title: Understanding Evergreen Alternative Funds
paragraphs: You may have heard the term "evergreen fund" as more alternative investment strategies adopt this structure. This note explains what that means, in plain terms, so any conversation with your advisor starts from a shared understanding.

Traditional private funds are closed-end. You commit capital, the manager calls it over time, invests it, and returns it years later when investments are sold. There is no way to add or withdraw money in between. Evergreen funds work differently. They are open-ended, meaning the fund continues indefinitely rather than winding down on a set schedule, and they offer periodic liquidity. In practice, this means the fund accepts new subscriptions and allows redemption requests at set intervals, often monthly or quarterly, rather than only at the end of a fixed term.

That periodic liquidity comes with limits. Funds can cap the amount redeemed in any given period, and in unusual market conditions they may reduce or pause redemptions altogether. This is a structural feature, not a flaw. It exists because the underlying investments, often private companies or real assets, cannot always be sold quickly or at a fair price on short notice. These limits exist so the fund is not forced into hurried sales of assets that take time to sell in an orderly way.

Evergreen structures also differ in how capital is put to work. Because the fund is continuously open, your investment can begin working right away rather than waiting for a manager to call committed capital over several years. This can simplify the experience of investing in private markets, though it does not eliminate the illiquidity that comes with holding private assets.

The main risks are worth stating clearly. Redemption limits mean you may not access all of your capital exactly when you want it. Valuations of private holdings are typically appraised periodically rather than priced daily, which introduces judgment into what a unit is worth at any given time. And the underlying investments carry the same business, market, and execution risks as any private investment.

None of this is a recommendation to own or avoid any particular structure. Whether an evergreen fund fits your portfolio depends on your liquidity needs, time horizon, and overall allocation. We would welcome a conversation with your advisor to talk through whether this is worth exploring further for you.

talking_points: Evergreen funds are open-ended vehicles with periodic subscription and redemption windows, unlike closed-end funds with a fixed term.
Redemptions are not guaranteed on demand. Funds can cap or pause them during periods of stress.
Client question: "Can I get my money out whenever I want?" Answer: No. Redemptions happen at set intervals and can be limited, so plan around that.
Client question: "Is this safer than a traditional private fund?" Answer: It is a different structure, not a safer one. The underlying assets carry the same risks.
Capital in an evergreen fund can typically begin working sooner, since there is no multi-year capital call period as with traditional closed-end funds.
Valuations for private holdings are periodic and involve appraisal judgment, not daily market pricing.
Client question: "Does this replace my private equity allocation?" Answer: Not necessarily. It's a different structure worth discussing in the context of your full allocation.
This is educational background only. Any decision should come from a conversation about your specific goals and liquidity needs.
